newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish premier battles floods and fierce criticism.
newsitem.headline: Polish premier battles floods and fierce criticism.

text.p: Poland's prime minister on Wednesday proposed new legislation to help victims cope with devastating floods this month and he defended his government's handling of the crisis against a fierce opposition attack in parliament.
Introducing 22 laws to rush funds and aid to hundreds of communities, Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said the worst was slowly ending and Polish society had withstood the test.
"This flood, which cannot be compared with anything in the past, has not thrown us on to our knees," he told an emergency session of the lower house.
Deputies began the gathering with a moment's silence for dozens of dead and hundreds of thousands whose homes and livelihoods have been wrecked.
Police put the death toll by late on Wednesday at 46 in the continuing floods, which began with torrential rains early last week.

Cimoszewicz said the damage was incalculable. Water had swamped 4,500 sq km (1,700 square miles), of which more than two-fifths were still inundated. It had affected 40,000 farms, 86 towns and 875 villages.
Reeling off a balance sheet of suffering, Cimoszewicz said 132,000 people had been forced to flee, and 72,000 of them had still not returned home.
He proposed bills including a change in the current budget to allow more borrowing at home and abroad, rapid cash payments to affected households, and reserve grain supplies to farmers.

Defending official responses to what he said had been an unexpectedly huge calamity, the ex-communist Cimoszewicz told deputies not to make political capital out of the crisis, to focus on current priorities and leave judgments for later.
But the opposition would not let him off the hook in the run-up to a general election on September 21 in which his Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) is challenged by a bloc led by the Solidarity union.
Centrist opposition leader Bronislaw Geremek said the government had failed the people in their hour of need.
"As a result of government inaction, the authority of
the state was eroded and weakened. Citizens' confidence in the state vanished," Geremek said, especially reproaching the government for failing to declare a state of emergency.
He said that if the cabinet had adopted emergency powers, it may have overcome the resistance of panicked local villagers and blown up dykes on the Odra River upstream from Wroclaw.

This would have flooded villages but may have saved the historic city of 650,000 people, still partially flooded on Wednesday, and other communities being struck by a slowly lessening wave surging north on the Odra, he said.

Cimoszewicz reassured Poles there had been no signs of contagious disease, only food poisoning, in areas where water was retreating to reveal smashed homes, broken bridges and chewed-up roads strewn with sewage and dead animals.

As the government faced a massive task of urgent relief and longer-term reconstruction, it walked a tightrope between the need for resources and the danger of harming economic stability -- underlined by the zloty's five percent fall on Tuesday.
On Wednesday the currency steadied somewhat.

To deal with the disaster's aftermath the government sought a 2.5 billion zloty ($710 million) credit line from the central bank and $300 million World Bank loan after it had already squeezed 650 million zlotys from exisiting budget resources.
It was unclear if voting on the bills that would make this borrowing and other steps possible would be over on Thursday or drag on into the weekend as the heated debate continued.
Cimoszewicz thanked countries rallying to Poland's aid, notably neighbouring Germany. The 15-nation European Union, of which Germany is a member, had asked him to draw up a list of needs.

Poland on Wednesday got the green light to begin EU entry talks, a triumph following hard on its inclusion among the first three former Soviet bloc states bound for membership in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation. The floods tarnished what otherwise would have been a national celebration of these diplomatic triumphs.
($ = 3.516 Polish Zlotys)
